media:content.media:description: Spigen Ultra Hybrid MagFit case for Pixel 11 and 11 Pro lifestyle
media:content.media:text: Spigen Ultra Hybrid MagFit case for Pixel 11 and 11 Pro lifestyle
media:content.media:title: Spigen Ultra Hybrid MagFit case for Pixel 11 and 11 Pro lifestyle

item.content:encoded:
Google has lifted the veil on the Pixel 11 series, and it's a fun color story across the board. The good news is, the base and Pro models share dimensions once again, measuring 6.0 in (height) x 2.8 in (width) x 0.3 in (depth), so the best Google Pixel 11 cases and the best Google Pixel 11 Pro cases are one and the same.

You might have spotted many first and third-party cases for the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro being sold separately. Don't worry about that, because you can use cases for either phone on the other. This just makes the color range even wider, so go ham on these awesome cases!

Dress up your Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro in a sleek, sturdy number
Google Pixelsnap Case for Pixel 11 & Pixel 11 Pro

Best overall

Google offers perfectly-fitted Pixelsnap cases with colors to match each of the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro's colorways. The first-party Google Pixelsnap Case is drop-tested for everyday drop and scratch protection, and it has a soft lining inside too.

Spigen Ultra Hybrid MagFit for Pixel 11

Best clear

The Spigen Ultra Hybrid MagFit is my favorite clear case because it outlasts far more expensive alternatives, clearly delivering superb value for money. It adds reasonable drop-proofing and works with wireless charging and magnetic accessories.
Bellroy Leather Case with Pixelsnap for Pixel 11 & Pixel 11 Pro

Best leather

The slim Bellroy Leather Case is officially Pixelsnap-compatible and comes in a range of colors that match the colorways of the Pixel 11 and the Pixel 11 Pro's official colorways. The hot pink Azalea is the most striking look, with the leather elevating its sleekness.

Poetic Revolution for Pixel 11 & Pixel 11 Pro

Best rugged

I have literally thrown this phone case from the second floor and my Pixel still survived in the military-grade Poetic Revolution case. For heavy-duty options, this is hands down the best Pixel 11 & Pixel 11 Pro case, and affordable too!

TORRAS Q3 Spin for Google Pixel 11 Pro

Best with ring stand

There are many useful cases offered by TORRAS, but the brand's slim Q3 Spin for Google Pixel 11 Pro stands out as the best case with a ring-shaped stand that also acts as a spinning phone holder. The cherry on top is that the ring is magnetic too!
Thinborne Pixel 11 Case

Best thin

The Thinborne Pixel 11 Case is miraculously thin, measuring only 0.09mm wide and weighing just 0.73 ounces light. This thin 600D Aramid Fiber case comes in black, blue, and red, and supports magnetic accessories.

FNTCASE Google Pixel 11 Pro Translucent Matte Case

Best color range

FNTCASE makes the cheapest Pixel 11 and 11 Pro case that covers all the basics and costs below $15. Most enticingly, it comes in a crazy range of 13 colors, all of which have a translucent matte finish with a magnetic ring on the back.
Case-Mate Floral Gems with Magnet Pixel 11 Case

Most fashionable

Case-Mate's Floral Gems with Magnet Pixel 11 Case is both stylish and protective, promising up to 12ft of drop protection for your Pixel 11. It has a transparent body mostly, adorned with glitzy florals and a glittery magnetic ring.

OtterBox Google Pixel 11 & Pixel 11 Pro Defender Series Pro Case

Best slim and tough

OtterBox is a cult classic case brand when it comes to heavy-duty protection. The brand has finessed its craft, delivering us this nautical-looking slim tough case that delivers seven times military-grade drop-proofing, as well as magnetic support.

  • Back to the top ^

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro case drip is too good

Hats off to the first and third-party case makers for the Google Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro, because the sheer variety of cases available is phenomenal. There are hundreds more where these came from, but I have selected only the best pick of the crop, especially considering the small nature of the two Pixel 11 models.

No matter your budget or your priority, there's an excellent Pixel 11 case for you on this list. Whether you want a clear magnetic case or something made of high-grade leather, I've got you covered.

If you don't know how to choose the right Pixel 11 case, think of your budget, whether you want the case to be heavy or light, and if you need extras like a stand or ring. The best overall Google Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro case is easily Google's own Pixelsnap Case, as it matches the Pixel 11 colorways perfectly, is made of recycled plastic, has a soft lining inside, and has Pixelsnap support. Not to mention, Google promises everyday drop and scratch resistance. It's good enough for any Pixel 11 or 11 Pro owner.

There are plenty of epic alternatives if you don't want to go with a first-party pick, including both tough cases and slim cases. Sift through the categories and find the right pick for your needs from the picks I've listed in this guide. Happy hunting!

item.title: One UI 9 Beta 5 is here, but rumors about what's next are living in our heads rent-free
item.description: Samsung started rolling out One UI 9 Beta 5 to enrolled Galaxy S26 testers in several overseas regions amid a One UI 9.5 rumor.
item.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz)
item.dc:creator: Nickolas Diaz

media:content.media:description: The back of the blue Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
media:content.media:text: The back of the blue Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
media:content.media:title: The back of the blue Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra

item.content:encoded:
What you need to know

  • One UI 9 Beta 5 is rolling out for enrolled Galaxy S26 testers in a few overseas regions with a 1.1GB download.
  • The patch carries a handful of fixes, alongside the August security update.
  • However, rumors on social media claim Samsung has started developing One UI 9.5 for the Galaxy S26, despite the main upgrade still in the Beta Program.

There's a lot happening today (Aug 12), but that's not stopping Samsung's beta program. Enrolled users, beware: Beta 5 is here.

This morning, the folks at SamMobile spotted the arrival of One UI 9 Beta 5 for the Galaxy S26 series. Currently, the beta has only been spotted in overseas countries: the U.K., South Korea, and India. This isn't unusual, as Samsung usually begins spreading its availability out little by little. Users in the U.S. should prepare for it to arrive later this week, if not the next. One UI 9 Beta 5 reportedly carries a 1.1GB download and the August 2026 security patch.

The publication highlights Samsung's patch notes, which highlight a few important fixes. It's fixing a "white screen" and "app freeze," which would occur for users when viewing "some menus" in Settings. What's more, Samsung is fixing a camera app issue when opened from the lock screen. Some users encountered lag or a black screen when attempting to open it.

Another fix is rolling out for the bottom floating bar when using the Phone app. Samsung received reports of it not appearing properly, which was reportedly patched. The remainder of the fixes are as follows:

  • Improved issue where a blank screen is temporarily visible when entering the recent files list in the My Files app
  • Improved issue where 1×1 size shortcuts are not added to the bottom bar of the home screen
  • Improved issue where the preview screen position is misaligned or flickers in the Video Editor and Photo Editor
  • Improved issue where the screen intermittently flickers in certain situations
  • Fixed Wi-Fi connection errors and improved connection stability

If you're enrolled in the One UI 9 Beta Program, keep your eyes out for the update in your respective region.

While this is interesting and gets us closer to launch for the Galaxy S26, rumors are already looking ahead to One UI 9.5. On X, tipster Tarun Vats reports that Samsung has started developing One UI 9.5 for the Galaxy S26 (via GSMArena). Vats says the early build sports version ending CZH1. Samsung has started development on its next major software update even earlier this time. Vats and users on X were quick to highlight Samsung's earlier schedule.

Vats reminds us that One UI 8.5's development began around September, before the Beta Program started for the Galaxy S25 in December. It's hard to forget that One UI 8.5 was heavily delayed throughout its Beta Program. Here's hoping that Samsung can avoid that this time around. Vats adds that Samsung likely won't roll out One UI 9.5 any time soon, meaning we may see it arrive around April or May 2027.

The beta rolls on

It's been nearly a month since the last One UI 9 beta. In mid-July, Samsung rolled out One UI 9 Beta 4, which included a host of fixes for early Android 17 problems. Much like what we're receiving in August, the July patch was ~1.25GB. One fix aimed to solve an issue with the S26 Ultra's Privacy Display routine. The feature would occasionally "not operate normally" while a routine was running. Other fixes involved an unstable UI for Live Notifications and other performance problems for the Quick Settings.

media:content.media:title: Hands-on with the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold

item.content:encoded:
Google's makes only one, large-form foldable every year. This time around, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes in just two colors, which is the same as every other Pixel foldable ever released. The shades aren't even radically different from the previous-gen Pixel 10 Pro Fold, which came in a light green option and another gray-ish colorway.

While the Pixel 11 Pro Fold doesn't come in a lighter colorway, it does offer one safe and one bold option, so anyone looking to own it is sure to be pleased. These are your options.

Your choice is simple: It's either green or black

Google
Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Olive

I'm loving the Pixel 11 Pro Fold in this darker, deeper olive green hue with gold accents. It is not too far away from the lighter Pixel 10 Pro Fold in Jade, and yet it is different enough to differentiate the two Pixel foldables.

Google
Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Obsidian

Unlike last year, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold actually offers a black colorway. This is also the only colorway that comes in a 1TB storage variant, and apart from the U.S., the only color option in most regions.

  • Back to the top ^

When picking a Pixel 11 Pro Fold color, ask yourself how much storage you want first

The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold comes in two colors, with one being a staple black colorway and the other being a more fun option. Obsidian is the classic black hue that is favored by many, and it is also the only Pixel 11 Pro Fold that is offered with 1TB storage. This actually makes your decision a little easier, even if it displeases some folks.

Right off the bat, you can eliminate the Pixel 11 Pro Fold in Olive if you want 1TB onboard. It makes sense to want that much memory if you're going to shell out two grand on a smartphone. You don't upgrade a phone like this every year either, so a generous amount of storage is a dire need for many.

However, if you're happy with 256GB and 512GB options, and prefer to be more daring in your choices, Olive is all style and glamour. This deep green Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold colorway comes with golden hardware, giving it an incredibly chic and luxurious air. If you want to make a statement, this is certainly the color to get.

media:content.media:title: Comparing the Google Pixel 11 with the Google Pixel 11 Pro

item.content:encoded:
The Google Pixel 11 series consists of the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL. The large-form foldable, Pixel 11 Pro Fold, was also launched alongside the three main devices. The lowest tier flagship, the Pixel 11, comes in slightly different colors, whereas the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL share the same shades.

If you're wondering which Google Pixel 11 color you should buy, you've come to the right place. Allow me to walk you through all the colorways of the Pixel 11 trio to help you decide.

The petite little Pixel 11 comes in four lively colors

Google
Pixel 11

Hibiscus

This hot pink shade is an eye-catching colorway for sure, and guaranteed to make heads turn. Even the rims of the camera bar match the body, making for a strikingly bold ensemble. This is also a color that's unique to the Pixel 11, as the other models don't have similar colors.

Google
Pixel 11

Pistachio

This understated, almost gray-toned green is a much warmer version of the olive green shade found on the other Pixel 11 models. Clearly, Google wanted the littlest Pixel 11 option to be brighter and more colorful than its upper-tier counterparts.

Google
Pixel 11

Frost

This is another Pixel 11 shade that isn't found on the more expensive Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL. In fact, none of the other Pixel 11 models even have a blue colorway. Frost is a pale, icy blue colorway that gives the Pixel 11 a serene look.

Google
Pixel 11

Obsidian

There's no way Google would ever skip the black option a smartphone release. After all, black colorways like the Pixel 11 in Obsidian sell the most for most smartphones. If you are a no-nonsense individual who can't deal with color, stick with this classic variant.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL come in the exact same squad of colors

Google
Pixel 11 Pro & Pixel 11 Pro XL

Canyon

One of two 1TB options for the Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL is Canyon, a pale coral shade that isn't quite as spunky or orange-y as the original coral colorway from the Pixel 6 era.

Google
Pixel 11 Pro & Pixel 11 Pro XL

Fog

If you're missing the mint colorway of the special Pixel 8 release, you'll love Fog on the Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL. This cool shade of green has a smokey air about it, almost like early morning mist.

Google
Pixel 11 Pro & Pixel 11 Pro XL

Olive

If you've ever taken a good, hard look at green olives, this is it. This is a second green shade, but it is much deeper and warm-toned in hue. It isn't, however, quite as warm or bright as the Pistachio shade found on the base model Pixel 11.

Google
Pixel 11 Pro & Pixel 11 Pro XL

Obsidian

This is the classic black colorway that's always found in flagships across the board, uniform across every smartphone brand almost. Both the Google Pixel 11 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL come in 1TB variants of Canyon and Obsidian alone.

  • Back to the top ^

Making the final decision about the right Pixel 11 colorway

All Google Pixel 11 models come with either 256GB or 512GB of storage, so you don't have to take that into consideration when thinking about which color to buy. However, when looking at the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL, only Canyon and Obsidian come with 1TB, while all the colors are available in 256GB and 512GB variants. This complicates things, as you're stuck with only two colors if you want to max out storage when buying a Pixel 11 series phone.

I'll make this really simple for you. If you want a Pixel 11 device with 1TB of storage, your only option is the Pixel 11 Pro or Pixel 11 Pro XL in Canyon or Obsidian. Naturally, the 11 Pro is cheaper, but the Pixel 11 Pro XL has a larger display, bigger battery, and faster wired charging.

Those of you who are interested in 256GB or 512GB variants will be happy to know that all colorways of the Pixel 11 are open for you to pick from. Know that Obsidian is the only matte shade across all Pixel 11 models, so that's another factor that makes your choice clear cut. If you don't want a glossy phone, pick Obsidian, the only color that's available on all three Pixel 11 models.

If you're looking for bolder shades, the basic Pixel 11 is better for you as it comes in a hot pink Hibiscus and bright green Pistachio. Canyon is another exciting colorway that is anything but dull, and Google paired it with 1TB memory on both the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL. And remember, it's your hard-earned money, so don't be shy about your choice. Pick a colorway that excites you!

item.content:encoded:
How fast is the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold charging speed?

Best answer: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes with a 30W or higher PPS charger. It now supports Qi2 (25W) wireless charging, which is 20% faster than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold.

Charging speed of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has improved, but at a big cost

Google is boasting about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the thinnest and lightest foldable it has produced, yet, but these gains have come at the cost of battery capacity. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 4,750mAh battery, which is 265mAh less than the 10 Pro Fold. While the weight has dropped drastically to 239 grams (from 258 grams), it's still not as light as the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra at 215 grams.

Battery life claims for the Pixel 11 Pro Fold seem to be the same as the 10 Pro Fold, where Google is promising "24+ hours" on one charge. Fast wired charging is the same as well as the previous model. The only real improvement that I can see if the addition of Qi2 (25W) wireless charging.

Google seems to be banking on the efficiency of the Tensor G6 SoC to make up for the loss in battery capacity, and I really hope it works out for its own sake. Google is on the back foot here when it comes to battery technology as Samsung and Motorola have both embraced silicon carbon battery tech for its respective 2026 foldables. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra packs a 5,000mAh battery capacity, while the Razr Fold has a 6,000mAh battery.

I think Google took a big gamble here, putting a smaller battery in the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Given its long-standing struggle trying to get Tensor to play nice with apps and its history with temperamental updates, this could go either way. I'm not sure if the Pixel 11 Pro Fold will make it to the list of the best Google Pixel phones, but maybe it will do better next year.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The lightest yet

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold finally gets comfortably slim and light, along with Qi2 (25) charging and the new HiLight feature. This is Google's best foldable to date and it has the price to match.

How fast is the Google Pixel 11 charging speed?

Best answer: The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro can reach up to 55% charge in 30 minutes with a 30W PPS charger, while the Pixel 11 Pro XL can reach up to 75% in the same time using a 45W PPS charger. All three models support Pixelsnap wireless charging, but now, even the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro support up to Qi2 (25W) wireless charging, in addition to the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Everything to know about the Google Pixel 11's battery and charging specs

Google unveiled the Pixel 11 series during its star-studded Made by Google event on August 12. Google is giving all three models a boost in battery life and wireless charging speeds, but it has also made some questionable changes to battery capacity in a few of them.

Let's start with the Pixel 11. Compared to the Pixel 10's 4,970mAh battery, the 11's battery gets a minor bump to 4,985mAh. Google now promises more than 30 hours of battery life for the 11, which is slightly higher than the 24 hour claim for the Pixel 10.

Fast charging time appears to be the same though as the Pixel 11 is rated to charge up to 55% in half an hour. Wireless charging speed for the Pixel 11 gets a big boost as it's now up to 25% faster, thanks to Qi2 (25W) support. The Pixel 10 only supported up to 15W Qi2 charging.

The Pixel 11 Pro gets a 4,850mAh battery, which is actually smaller than the Pixel 10 Pro's 4,870mAh battery, though not by much. Wired charging claims for the 11 Pro are similar to the Pixel 11, but wireless charging is now up to 29% faster when compared to the 10 Pro.

Lastly, the Pixel 11 Pro XL gets the biggest reduction in battery capacity, to 5,115mAh, compared to the 5,200mAh in the 10 Pro XL. That's a big 85mAh difference. Just like the 10 Pro XL, the 11 Pro XL can once again charge the quickest in a 30-minute dash, all the way up to 75%. Wireless charging speed has also improved up to 17% compared to the 10 Pro XL, but the latter already supported Qi2 (25W).

The slightly smaller battery capacities in the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL doesn't seem to have affected Google's battery life claims, and I'm hoping the same is true during real-world usage as well. The improved efficiency claims of the Tensor G6 and faster wireless charging should help the Pixel 11 series become the best Google Pixel phones we've seen, yet.

Shinning brightly

The Pixel 11 Pro XL promises the best battery life and has the quickest charging in the series. Coupled with the new cameras and HiLight feature, and the 11 Pro XL might just be the best large-screen Pixel, yet.

item.content:encoded:
Is the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 waterproof?

Best answer: No, neither the Galaxy Z Fold 8 nor the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are waterproof. Both phones have IP48 certification, which means they are water-resistant out of the box and can be submerged in up to 1.5 meters of water for up to 30 minutes. However, water resistance is not a permanent condition and will degrade over time.

Everything you need to know about Galaxy Z Fold 8 durability

First things first, no smartphone is completely waterproof. Many flagships are water resistant, but this does not mean they are fully protected against liquid ingress. Instead, the water-resistance level of a phone is measured using the International Protection (IP) standard. When you look at an IP rating like IP68 or IP69, the first digit signifies the device's dust protection while the second digit denotes the device's liquid protection.

IP68 and IP69 are currently the highest levels of the International Protection (IP) standard. The "6" in IP68 and IP69 means a device is completely dustproof. The number "8" as the second digit means a device can withstand submersion in up to 1.5 meters of freshwater depth for up to 30 minutes. The number "9" as the second digit in IP69 means a device could survive high-pressure and high-temperature water jets in addition to the submersion depth and duration specified by the "8" in IP68.

With that background in place, we can evaluate the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's IP48 certification. This rating means neither the Galaxy Z Fold 8 nor the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are completely dustproof. Instead, both devices are merely protected against the ingress of dust particles larger than 1mm in size. But what about their water resistance?

The "8" in IP48 indeed means the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra both meet the highest International Protection (IP) level for submersion. Both phones can withstand submersion in up to 1.5 meters of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. Note that your mileage may vary with salt water submersion (like in the ocean) or chlorinated water submersion (like in a pool). Additionally, these phones do not support IPX9, meaning they are not protected against high-temperature or high-pressure water jets.

Keep in mind that water resistance is not a permanent condition. Samsung only guarantees IP48 certification when your device leaves the factory and arrives at your door. As the company explains in a support document, you can expect the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's water resistance to diminish over time.

Samsung Galaxy phones feature water resistance ratings like IP68, IPX8, and IP54, designed to protect against accidental water exposure. However, water resistance is not permanent and can degrade over time due to wear, damage, or improper handling. Understanding your device's rating and following proper care guidelines can help maintain its protection.

Samsung

To sum up, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are highly water-resistant. However, this doesn't mean you should rush to use your foldables in the water. The phones' IP48 ratings only guarantee water resistance in specific conditions, and only at the time you buy them. Every drop wears down the rubber seals inside your phone that keep liquid out, and the seals degrade over time even if kept in perfect condition.

Galaxy Z Fold 8

Best for content

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 features a wider aspect ratio that makes the inner display perfect for watching videos and playing games. It's also the lightest Samsung big-screen foldable to date. It isn't waterproof, however.

Samsung
Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

Samsung's flagship foldable

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is Samsung's best foldable ever, with an upgraded rear camera system and a larger silicon-carbon battery. That said, it's still not completely waterproof.

Google Pixel 11 Qi2 wireless charging support: Here's what you need to know

If you've been thinking about getting a flagship Android phone soon, you just got a few more fantastic options to select from, as the latest Google Pixel 11 series has arrived. The line-up includes three feature-loaded slab-style smartphones, as well as a premium foldable. As you'd expect, all the devices bring a bunch of upgrades over their respective predecessors, both in terms of hardware and software.

When it comes to external design, the Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL are dead ringers for the trio they succeed, right down to dimensions. Arguably the biggest "Hilight" (pun intended) here is the multi-colored ambient LED array on the camera bar. All three devices are powered by Google's freshest Tensor G6 SoC, which is claimed to be up to 20 percent more energy-efficient over the previous-gen chipset. Also, wired charging speeds continue to remain the same (up to 30W on the Pixel 11 and the Pixel 11 Pro, and up to 45W on the Pixel 11 Pro XL) on the trio, provided you have/buy a USB-C wall charger up to the task.

Also, integrated magnets allow full compatibility with Google's Pixelsnap and a range of other Qi2 accessories.

This is always a tough question whenever new phones come out. On the one hand, I'm generally of the opinion that manufacturers don't need to be producing new phones every single year, particularly when most flagship releases come with seven years of OS upgrades as standard.

If you already own the Google Pixel 10, you won't see a massive upgrade with the Pixel 11. I'd only jump to the new phone if you're particularly interested in the latest and greatest Pixel experience.

If, on the other hand, you own an older device and can score a good deal through the channels listed above, then by all means go for it. After all, these phones are sure to rank among the best Android phones ever built, so you won't be disappointed.

item.content:encoded:
Google
Pixel 11 Pro Fold

A great choice

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is built on Gemini Intelligence, and it comes with all the AI-enabled features you'll ever want. It also has a new camera and unique shooting modes, and Google doubled down on unique extras to make it stand out.

Samsung
Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

Nothing but the best

With the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Samsung proved once again why it is the best at foldables. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is sleeker and thinner than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold while having a bigger battery, you get better cameras, great software features, and useful extras.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Pricing and availability

While there are plenty of differences between these two foldables, the one area where they're similar is the pricing. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs the same for the 256GB model. Both foldables are available with up to 1TB of storage, and come with decent trade-in offers if you're in the U.S.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Design

Both brands have their own visual identity, and that's reflected in their latest foldables. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold looks nearly identical to its predecessor, and other than a slightly redesign around the rear camera island, the design is unchanged.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra shares a lot of similarities with last year's Z Fold 7, and that's a good thing. It's also 23g lighter than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold at 215g, and that makes a difference. And at just 8.9mm folded, it is a lot thinner than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold's 10.1mm. Clearly, Samsung has the advantage when it comes to quantifiable metrics, but I prefer the in-hand feel of the Pixel; Google's foldable has a rounded design that nestles better in the hand, and I like the design a little better.

Both foldables have 6.5-inch OLED outer panels and 8-inch OLED inner panels, and they have the same 120Hz refresh. I'll need to do qualitative testing, but the Pixel 11 Pro Fold should be brighter in real-world usage — this was the case last year as well. Both phones have a crease that isn't noticeable, and neither is quite as good as the Find N6 at this.

Google also wins when it comes to ingress protection; the Pixel 11 Pro Fold gets IP68 dust and water resistance, while the Z Fold 8 Ultra is IP48. I'm guessing the added resilience contributed to the increase in weight.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Hardware and cameras

Like previous years, Samsung absolutely dominates the hardware side of things. Thanks to a bigger 5,000mAh battery, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra manages to last a day without issues. Google put a smaller 4,750mAh battery in the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and I still don't understand why it did that — a bigger battery is always preferable.

There's also the small matter of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra being faster than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and even though Google went with the Tensor G6 this year, it isn't quite on the same level as Qualcomm's best silicon.

Samsung arguably has better cameras; the 200MP main camera on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra stands out, and is one of the best you can get on a foldable today. Google is using a new 48MP camera on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold (thankfully), and it's safe to say that it will be much better than what we got in the last two years.

That said, Google hasn't changed the auxiliary sensors, and Samsung has a distinct advantage. Google is touting unique features like Magic Capture and Camera Looks to differentiate its cameras, and I'll test how the foldable holds up against the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Find N6 soon.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Software

Google always had the edge with software, and that isn't changing. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold debuts with Gemini Intelligence, an agentic AI that handles mundane tasks on your behalf. I'll have to use it to see if it's any good at doing so, but when it comes to on-device AI, there isn't another brand that can measure up to what Google is doing.

Samsung has its own suite of Galaxy AI features, and they're great in their own right. One UI 9 based on Android 17 also has a lot to like, but I prefer Google's take on software.

Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Which should you buy?

Samsung continues to lead the way in foldable tech, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a grand showcase. It has better battery life, cameras, and a sleeker design, and is the safe bet.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold may not look like it, but it is a good all-rounder too, and it's the one I'd want to use even if it doesn't have the best cameras or class-leading battery.

Samsung nailed it with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and this is the best foldable you can buy in the U.S. It has a svelte design, big battery, great cameras, vibrant AMOLED panels inside and out, a new hinge that doesn't have a noticeable crease, and one of the best software interfaces around.

What you need to know

  • With the Pixel 11 launch upon us, Google highlights a plethora of features, such as Gemini's Rambler for voice input, cutting out filler words, and "multi-step task" action.
  • Gemini will also produce useful information as it happens, so if you're talking to a friend about a trip, the AI would offer flight details and more.
  • The Pixel camera plays a major role, providing even quicker Instant Night Sight and "Camera Look," which lets users choose the ideal aesthetic for every photo they take.

The Pixel 11 series is finally here, and Google is highlighting a handful of features that tie its eventful debut together.

As you might expect, Gemini is taking center stage on Google's Pixel 11 series. The company highlights several updates for the phones that bring "personalized updates" with everyday tasks. Gemini Intelligence is taking a step forward on the Pixel 11 with the capability to handle "multi-step tasks" across "your favorite apps." Since Gemini Intelligence is expanding to over 40 apps with the Pixel 11, the company foresees even more usefulness from this personalized feature.

Rambler, Gemini's voice input feature, is included in this. Rambler can remove filler words from your speech, such as "um" or "ah." What's new with Rambler joins a set of updates for Gboard on the Pixel 11. Sign-to-text is the app's next major feature that lets users who rely on sign language uniquely send messages.

On a helpful note, Google says Gemini can "offer timely, helpful information through easily glanceable cards in the apps you’re already using." It states that, if you're talking about a trip with a friend, Gemini might produce a card on your screen with booking details, stating whether your flight is on time or delayed. More suggestions based on the conversations you're having will be a constant for Gemini, whether you're chatting about a trip or about dinner.

Google teases one more thing: location-based insights. This is only launching in preview for now in the Gemini app. Google states that you might see insights about a restaurant you're at. If so, on your lock screen, Gemini would push menu items or where people commonly sit.

So much for this camera

You can't forget the Pixel 11's camera. The phones boast a series of camera-focused updates that should help users, such as "Camera Looks." Users can set how their pictures look by default, choosing among Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla (golden-glow aesthetic). If you're looking for "Natural," Google says you'll find more relaxed details, while "Shadows" offers deeper contrast. The options don't end there, as the Pixel 11 offers even more camera aesthetics: Digi, Black Tie, Minimal, Editorial, Classic, and Velvet.

You should always try to have enough light when you're taking pictures, but for moments when you don't, that's where the Pixel 11's Low-Light capabilities come into play. Instant Night Sight on the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL is ~4.5 times faster. Elsewhere, the Creator Suite has been enhanced to help content creators quickly find tools in the camera's viewfinder. Users can then save their content (i.e., captured videos) to video project folders for safekeeping.

Then, we have Magic Capture. Google says this feature is designed for those "blink-and-you’ll-miss-it baby smiles, playful pets, or hard-to-get action shots." Magic Capture leans on the phone's on-device intelligence and Gemini to capture 400 frames or "high-quality" 12MP photos that are ready to share. What's more, it will also provide a video for users.

Circle to Search is also headed to the Pixel camera, and real-time audio and video translations arrive for Live Translate.

You've been waiting all week, and now the Google Pixel 11 series is officially here!

As expected, the lineup includes the Google Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold, plus the Pixel Watch 5 and the surprise Pixel Tag.

  • Hands-on with the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL
  • Hands-on with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold
  • Hands-on with the Pixel Watch 5

But here's the kicker:

We got early hands-on time with the Pixel 11 devices, which were publicly revealed hours before the Made by Google keynote, which aired later in the evening.

In other words, we gave you a sneak peek at everything that Trevor Noah, Stephen Curry, Shubman Gill, Ayami Nakajo, and others have announced and demoed during today's event!

We hope you enjoyed the keynote, and you can scroll through our live blog to see the coolest new features you're going to love, from our short experiences with the Pixel 11 series to the reveals and demos from the Made by Google keynote (as well as our reactions).

When and what time is Made by Google?

The Made by Google keynote began Wednesday, August 12, at 3 p.m. PT / 6 p.m. EDT.

How to watch the Made by Google event?

Google streamed the event on its official Made by Google YouTube Channel. You could also watch it live on the Google Store website. Click the video below to watch the keynote and get all the highlights, or follow our live blog for our reactions from the event!

August 12, 2026 – 10:02 AM

We know our readers are long-time Pixel fans, and because of that, I'm confident that you're going to love the Pixel 11 Pro. The Pro has been my favorite model of the lineup for the past two years, and that's undoubtedly going to continue with the Pixel 11 series, as well.

As with the Pixel 9 and 10 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro packs all the same great power as the Pixel 11 Pro XL, just in a smaller package. Google remains one of the only companies making a proper Pro model at this size, all without cutting back on processing power, RAM, or camera capabilities.

August 12, 2026 – 10:05 AM

Above, you can see the Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro. The 11 Pro is on the right, featuring a fuller camera bar with edge-to-edge glass on the back. Google is also leaning into the "glitz and glamor" of the Pixel design with bold new colors and a gorgeous gold/copper trim around the sides. Jade was my favorite colorway last year, and this year goes all-in on the aesthetic.

Aside from the glassier (is that a word?) camera bar, Google swapped out the temperature sensor and replaced it with HiLight, a new circular LED array that looks like an LED flash at first, but adds much more function than a simple flash can.

August 12, 2026 – 10:08 AM

In the video above, we tested out the new HiLight feature by asking Gemini about the weather. Sure, it's a pretty boring prompt, but the idea here is to see how the HiLight LED swirls and changes color based on what Gemini is doing.

When it's idle, HiLight is a solid color. As you ask Gemini something, it'll start swirling around in a specific pattern, change that pattern as Gemini is processing the request, then have a totally different pattern as Gemini is speaking.

August 12, 2026 – 10:11 AM

But that's not all HiLight is good for! HiLight can glow with different colors and patterns when you receive notifications, phone calls, messages, and more. Plus, it's fully customizable, so you can toy around with it to your heart's content. It reminds us an awful lot of the LEDs that Nothing puts on the back of its phones, and Google says the idea is to keep you off your screen more by giving you simple, glanceable updates when your phone is face-down.

August 12, 2026 – 10:13 AM

HiLight is included in the camera bar on all Pro models. That includes:

  • Google Pixel 11 Pro
  • Google Pixel 11 Pro XL
  • Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Despite having a similar-looking white LED module on the back, the base Google Pixel 11 (pictured above) only features an LED flash. HiLight is considered a "Pro feature" this year, so you'll have to make do without it if you opt for the less expensive Pixel 11.

August 12, 2026 – 10:17 AM

Pixels are definitely premium-level devices, but Google rarely pushes the boundaries of processing power in a traditional way with them. Instead, the Tensor G6 inside all Pixel 11 family phones (yes, even the base Pixel 11) features a 50% faster TPU for local AI processing enhancements. While that could result in something boring like faster Gemini responses, Google is using it for some impressive software tricks, instead.

In the video above, you can watch Magic Capture in action. This new Pixel camera feature can be found by swiping up on the camera viewfinder. Once you hit start, Magic Capture will record what the camera sees, then use Tensor to select the best moments from that timeline.

Photos are automatically saved based on facial expressions, action and movement, and other key factors, all with HDR+ quality. That's going to elevate Pixel even further as the camera to have for parents and pet lovers!

August 12, 2026 – 10:20 AM

This frame, in particular, is unbelievably impressive to me. As the gentleman was juggling, Gemini understood that we wanted pictures of what he was doing, not just when he was smiling. That gave us a perfect photo of the balls in the air mid-juggle, and I absolutely cannot wait to test this out in other scenarios when my Pixel 11 Pro arives!

August 12, 2026 – 10:23 AM

The next ridiculously impressive feature is Live Video Translate, but it's not at all what you think. We already have ways of enabling closed captions and language translation through YouTube, but the Pixel 11 series can do all this in real-time.

In the example above, we start playing a video that has original Spanish audio. Pixel understands that English is the main language (something you select in setup) and will automatically translate the person's voice live as you're watching it. It feels like something straight out of the future, and it's possible thanks to Tensor G6's more powerful TPU.

August 12, 2026 – 10:25 AM

Gemini on Pixel can now also create entire workout regimines for you with a simple prompt. Let's say you're like me and are having IT band pain. Just ask Gemini for a 20-minute workout to help relieve IT band pain and it'll come up with an entire workout set for you.

Impressively, this isn't just words or a list of stuff to do. It's an entirely interactive "app" with rep counts and health logging that can go straight to Google Health. It even includes generated videos of each workout, so you don't have to guess what you're doing!

August 12, 2026 – 10:27 AM

Circle to Search is getting the upgrade everyone has been asking for: Circle to Search in Camera. This new camera mode goes beyond what using Circle to Search can already do by creating a dedicated camera mode, similar to how Google Lens has worked in the past. The big difference here is that you can circle what you're looking at rather than just point the camera and hope Gemini understands.

August 12, 2026 – 10:34 AM

Tensor G6 plus the new camera hardware is also enabling Google to improve Night Sight to a point that we haven't yet seen. Night Sight is now instant, and Google measures this as 4.5x faster than previous Pixels. That's a wild number, and certainly an improvement we don't often see generation-over-generation!

August 12, 2026 – 10:38 AM

Before we move on from cameras, let's look at the hardware upgrades for the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL. Google has swapped out the main and telephoto sensors on the back with all-new ones. Here's the quick breakdown:

  • Main: NEW 50MP 1/1.3" sensor with f/1.68 aperture
  • Ultrawide: 48MP 1/2.51" sensor with f/1.7 aperture
  • Telephoto: NEW 48MP 1/1.95" sensor with f/2.8 aperture
  • Selfie: 42MP dual PD autofocus with f/2.2 aperture
August 12, 2026 – 10:40 AM

Oh gosh, and how could I forget about the new and improved video capture? Google has been listening to feedback and worked really hard to improve video capture quality on this year's Pixels. That includes what Google says is the "best video quality ever on a Pixel," as well as a new Pro Stable video mode that we're hoping will rival what Samsung and Motorola have been doing for a while.

August 12, 2026 – 10:43 AM

But the absolute coolest new video feature is the Creator Suite, which turns the Pixel 11 family into the only phone you're going to want to make videos on. As the name implies, Creator Suite has a full suite of capabilities for your next big social media posts, including the ability to organize videos into project folders, refine videos in a special storyboard mode, and even display your script in an on-screen teleprompter while recording the video! It's crazy awesome, and I can't wait to make videos on it.

August 12, 2026 – 10:46 AM

The whole Pixel 11 family sports some truly fantastic colors, with pink, green, and blue as the sort of "hero colors" for the line. As with some previous models, the base Pixel 11 features the most vibrant colors, while the Pro line is a bit more muted. I'd say I guess pros are boring, but these colors are far from the usual bland white and black we typically see.

And the colors aren't the only thing that you'll love about the new build. Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL both ship with Gorilla Glass Victus 2, and Google says the displays are now 2x more scratch resistant than any Pixel before it.

August 12, 2026 – 10:47 AM

And those gorgeous new colors shine super bright on the base Pixel 11, where Google clearly turned the color palette up to 11.

August 12, 2026 – 10:53 AM

The base Pixel 11 sees the smallest number of upgrades this year, but that doesn't mean it's getting nothing. Google swapped out the main camera sensor on the back with a new 48MP sensor that pulls in 56% more light than the Pixel 10's sensor. Plus, Google improved the telephoto camera to hit 30x zoom now, thanks to Gemini's intelligent imaging algorithms.

August 12, 2026 – 10:57 AM

And let's not forget about the Pixel 11 Pro Fold! This one uses a similar design language to the Pixel 9 and 10 Pro Folds, with a slightly elongated camera bar to fit HiLight in.

August 12, 2026 – 10:59 AM

You can see the Pixel 10 Pro Fold and Pixel 11 Pro Fold above. The 11 Pro Fold has the prominent HiLight LED on the camera bar, plus more glass on the overall housing. Google improved the Pixel 11 Pro Fold's cameras with a new 48MP main sensor it says pulls in 56% more light (looks like it's the same sensor on the regular Pixel 11), plus a return of the 10.5MP ultrawide and 10.8MP 5x telephoto cameras on the back.

August 12, 2026 – 11:02 AM

Maybe most importantly, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now 1mm thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, a difference you can clearly see in the picture above. Impressively, Google kept Pixelsnap inside all four models, including the way thinner 11 Pro Fold, so you can enjoy MagSafe accessories with or without a case.

August 12, 2026 – 11:03 AM

And that new back isn't glass; it's a composite material that Google says is impossible to crack. Considering I just put a foldable phone through a mud bath and a dishwasher cycle, I'm absolutely going to be testing that claim to see if it's true.

August 12, 2026 – 11:09 AM

All Pixel 11 models ship with Rambler, an upgraded Gemini-powered speech-to-text engine that allows you to simply talk to your phone instead of planning out a dialog. This includes removing parts of speech like "ums" and "uhs," as well as giving your text proper formatting based on anunciation. You can even back things up by saying "actually, nevermind" or something similar, which Gemini will understand as a mistake and correct what you previously said.

August 12, 2026 – 11:13 AM

Alright, enough of the phones for now. Let's spend a little time with the Pixel Watch 5, shall we? If you love the look of the Pixel Watch, that's great, because there's zero visual difference between this year's Watch and last year's. Personally, I'm happy with that, given that Google's design language is completely different from every other smartwatch on the market.

August 12, 2026 – 11:21 AM

Here are two of the Pixel Watch 5 colorways, gorgeous as ever. The new CPU inside is 20% faster and has 50% more RAM, so Google was able to pack in a bunch of new Gemini features that would otherwise be difficult on a smartwatch.

August 12, 2026 – 11:22 AM

Google also upgraded the GPS accuracy and health monitoring tools on this year's watch. GPS tracking is said to be 2x more accurate than before, and Google claims it's better than the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.

Pixel Watch 5 also features breathing emergency alerts, blood pressure trends, and insulin resistance trends for a more accurate health profile.

August 12, 2026 – 11:25 AM

The new health trends are based on 30-day summaries, not real-time data. This means you can't quickly check your blood pressure or insulin resistance at the drop of a dime, but it does mean that Gemini works to process all that data captured over a full month and deliver summaries and actionable information that might be more important in the long run.

August 12, 2026 – 11:27 AM

Google's upgraded At A Glance widget now surfaces even more information thanks to Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions. This might be as simple as a floating reminder for an upcoming calendar event, the next turn for your Google Maps directions, or an important reminder you accidentally dismissed.

August 12, 2026 – 11:29 AM

Watchfaces will never be the same again, thanks to Gemini. Now, you can ask Gemini to create entire watchfaces for you, and in 30 seconds or so, that custom watchface will pop on the beautiful OLED display. Check the video above for to see it in action during our hands on!

August 12, 2026 – 11:32 AM

And it might have taken 84 years, but Google finally added a proper way to count reps and sets in your strength training workouts. One of my biggest pet-peeves with Wear OS over the years is that none of these watches ever included such a basic feature — you always had to find a 3rd party app on the Play Store for that. Now, that's FINALLY fixed, and Google's new workout builder feature goes hand-in-hand with the similar feature on the Pixel 11 to creat the ultimate at-home workout coach.

August 12, 2026 – 11:35 AM

Lastly, is the Google Pixel Tag. Google didn't spend much time on this product, but it's an obvious extension of the Find Hub functionality built into Android. Pixel Tag weighs 11.8g and is IP67 rated, so it fits nicely on a keyring, bag, or anything you want to ensure can be tracked once lost.

Pixel Tag features UWB and Bluetooth support and functions up to 50 meters from the paired phone. The big miss here is that you have to purchase a separate keyring attachment to get the keyring hole, otherwise, Pixel Tag is just a little silver puck.

August 12, 2026 – 11:36 AM

Pixel Tag is coming on November 11 and sells individually for $29. You can get a discount by buying four at a time, which will run $99. A replaceable CR2032 battery is inside and should last over a year at a time.

August 12, 2026 – 11:43 AM

As with most electronics, the Pixel Watch 5 is getting a bit of a price increase. The base 41mm Bluetooth-only model starts at $399, while the 45mm model starts at $429. If you want one with LTE connectivity, you're looking at $499 and $529, respectively. There's even a Stephen Curry Edition Pixel Watch 5 coming alongside the crew, retailing for $579. All models launch on September 3.

Here's everything you need to know about the Pixel Watch 5!

August 12, 2026 – 11:46 AM

The Pixel 11 series is also seeing a bit of a price increase, but in a roundabout way on some models. What you need to know

  • The Pixel Buds Pro 2 now actively adjust noise cancellation in real time to counteract subtle shifts or seal slips during movement.
  • Audio settings like EQ adjustments (such as boosting bass) can now be toggled on demand using simple voice commands.
  • Tapping an earbud activates near real-time listening for over 70 languages, while your connected Pixel phone can broadcast your spoken response back in the target language.

Google’s new earbuds are leaving hardware updates behind in favor of smarter software tricks. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a, which debuted today alongside the Pixel 11 series, are receiving a set of hands-free features to make the earbuds much more adaptable for daily use starting this fall.

The big upgrade is Dynamic ANC, which addresses a surprisingly common issue with earbuds: your fit can change while you’re wearing them. The first-generation Pixel Buds Pro used the standard Silent Seal tech for active noise canceling.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 can now handle slight changes to the seal to keep noise cancelation stronger. That sounds like a useful extension of the Pro 2's existing ANC system, which Google says already cancels up to twice as much noise as the original Pixel Buds Pro.

Google is bringing Gemini closer to the controls, too. You can use your voice to change settings, like telling Google to turn up the bass without having to grab your phone.

Sleep tracking is getting a Pixel ecosystem boost. A Pixel Watch can detect when you’ve gone to sleep and pause playback, turn off touch controls, and mute notifications.

Live Translate is another major leap forward. Pressing the Buds switches you to listening mode so you can get the gist of more than 70 languages in near real time without handling your phone. You can also speak normally and have your Pixel phone say the translated response to the other person.

The hardware is still familiar. The Pro 2 is 27% smaller and 24% lighter than the original Pixel Buds Pro, and it comes with Google’s Tensor A1 chip and a redesigned fit.

Additionally, there's a new Olive finish. Orders will open August 12, with software features rolling out starting in September.

What you need to know

  • Compatible Pixel phones can now share contacts, photos, videos, and more when you bring two devices together.
  • Exchanging contacts works straight from the home screen via an instant two-way exchange, while sending media requires just opening the Share Sheet and bumping phones.
  • The feature goes live starting today for Pixel 6 and newer devices, with Samsung's new Fold 8 and Flip 8 lineup next in line.

Google is making it easier to share content between Android devices. Starting today, compatible Pixel phones can use Quick Share to exchange contact information, photos, videos, and more simply by bringing the devices close together.

The new tap-to-share feature builds on Quick Share, Google's existing Android sharing system, but removes some of the usual friction. Now, you don’t have to go digging through menus when you’re exchanging contact info. From the home screen, pair two compatible Android devices and they can start a two-way exchange.

Media sharing is a little bit different. On your phone, open the Share Sheet, then move the two devices together to send the selected photos or videos. Google says the feature is meant to make it easier to share between Android phones, especially when you’re passing content or contact info to someone nearby.

There is one catch: availability is limited for now. Google says the feature is rolling out for Pixel 6 and newer devices starting today. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 are next, with support coming soon.

However, Google has plans to continue expanding the new feature. The company says tap-to-share will be rolled out to more Android devices by the end of the year. That would make Quick Share a much more natural part of the Android experience, especially when you’re sending something to the person standing right beside you.

item.content:encoded:
If you asked me a few years ago about my thoughts on foldable devices, I would have given you the stank face and said they suck. I would then proceed to convince you that foldable devices feel cheap and aren’t worth the money.

I have since completely changed my mind on them. In the past two years alone, I have seen some of the most premium-looking and feeling foldables on the market. And, while I think Google has always nailed it when it comes to their foldables, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold really isn’t a nominal difference from what it was last year.

I had some early hands-on time with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and while there are a few upgrades, overall, I thought the phone itself was pretty much identical to its predecessor.

I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again: this is the year Google needs to focus on perfecting Gemini, and it did. I am glad that Google decided to really ensure that what you’re getting in the Pro models of the phones is what you’re really paying for.

Go thin or go home

This year’s trend across all companies making foldable devices is: how can we make our foldables even thinner? I much prefer a curvaceous body, but on a phone, I don’t want to compromise on thickness. The thinner the better, so long as the phone itself feels premium and comfortable.

The 11 Pro Fold is about 1mm thinner than its predecessor, which says one thing to me: companies are going to keep trying to push the boundaries to see how thin they can make a foldable without compromising on features.

You might not think this is going far enough, especially following the recent launch of the even thinner Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. However, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold still has some things going for it that the Ultra doesn’t have, such as built-in Qi2 magnetic charging, which definitely adds to its thickness.

But in addition to making the phone thinner, Google also launched the Pixel 11 Pro Fold in a new colorway. The beautiful Olive variant similar to the Pro and Pro XL models. And my god, the color is stunning. Holding it feels so sexy; it is truly a beautiful phone.

Crease? What crease?

Part of why I really didn’t like foldable devices in the past is because the inside screen has to be some sort of plastic; it can’t be glass; that is the only way it’s going to be a device that can fold. But I found that this felt so tacky and low-grade, and when you’re spending an arm and a leg for a device, why would you want a big screen that looked…cheap?

I can say without a doubt that the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s crease is near non-existent. And even the actual feel of the screen feels so lush, premium, and gorgeous. After closing and opening the phone a few times, you can barely tell that there’s a crease, and I think that the phone itself feels so exquisite.

When folded laptop style on your desk, I can see how convenient it would be to watch YouTube videos and whatnot.

That said, using the Pixel 11 Pro Fold while folded flat still feels a bit awkward to me. I get the appeal of doing it; you have a much larger screen, and I think if you folded it flat and held it in your hands, you’d be fine. But when placed on a table, that protruding camera bump makes your camera feel like a wobbly table that annoyingly moves around when you’re sitting at it.

Features galore

Like the Pixel 11 Pro phones, the Fold will also get all of the same premium features that are super fun to use.

HiLight is going to be a fun feature to use when you want to ask Gemini something or when you get notifications. The feature itself is a small LED glowing light that emits from the LED module on the camera bar.

Google also highlights a new sign language-to-text feature for Google Translate, and while I didn’t get to try this during my hands-on, it’s a very compelling feature that should make Pixels much more accessible.

I can’t stop thinking about the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

It’s been a busy several weeks of new launches, and coming from just having played around with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra…I can’t help but say that I think that phone has my heart.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is much thinner than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold; it’s sleeker, and I actually think it looks and feels like a much more premium device than the Pro Fold. This isn’t me hating on the 11 Pro Fold at all… but when I was at my content capture, I couldn’t stop thinking about the Z Fold 8 Ultra.

I kinda felt like I was cheating on it with the 11 Pro Fold. I kept thinking about the beautiful deep purple color variant, and how gorgeous she was as a device.

Thinking so much about the Z Fold 8 Ultra and the smaller Fold 8 made me wonder if Google needs to think about how it plans on evolving the form factor of its foldable. And maybe that’s something the company wants to think about for 2027. Because I will say, as gorgeous as the 11 Pro Fold is, it’s still boring. And if I am thinking about a different device the whole time, then something is wrong.

What you need to know

  • The Pixel Tag debuts alongside the Pixel 11 series as Google’s first in-house Bluetooth tracker.
  • The thin, oval-shaped Pixel Tag weighs just 11.8g and carries an IP67 rating, but it lacks a built-in keyring hole.
  • Google taps its network of more than 1 billion Android devices to help locate lost items beyond Bluetooth range.
  • UWB and Bluetooth Channel Sounding provide distance and directional guidance, with UWB working up to 50 meters from the paired phone.

Google is finally stepping into the Bluetooth tracker race. The search giant has unveiled the Pixel Tag along with its Pixel 11 series at today’s Made by Google event.

The Pixel Tag combines the Find Hub network with Ultra Wideband and Bluetooth Channel Sounding. It’s a departure from the circular disk design of its competitors and takes a thin oval pebble-like shape in a color simply called "Fog." It weighs roughly 0.4 ounces and has an IP67 water and dust resistance rating.

However, there’s one very major design choice that could split opinions: there’s no dedicated keyring hole. Like the AirTag, you’ll need to purchase a separate case to attach it to your keys.

Software-wise, the Pixel Tag is tightly integrated with Google’s Find Hub network. It’s basically a more advanced Find My Device system that leverages a network of over a billion Android devices to create a crowdsourcing location network. It employs Fast Pair for quick setup.

The basics are familiar if you’ve been using a Bluetooth tracker. Attach the Pixel Tag to your keys, wallet, or luggage, then use the Find Hub app to find it on a map or trigger the built-in speaker to sound.

Google also lets you share a tag with up to 10 people, which could come in handy for shared keys, bags, or other household items. Setup is handled through Android’s Fast Pair and works with phones running Android 9 or newer.

Compatible Android phones can use Ultra Wideband and Bluetooth Channel Sounding for precision finding, providing distance and directional cues instead of making you wander around while listening for a beep. Channel Sounding requires Android 16 and Bluetooth 6.0, while UWB precision finding requires a compatible UWB-enabled Android device and works up to 50 meters away from the paired phone.

But what really makes the Pixel Tag stand out is the built-in button that lets you ring your phone in reverse. You don’t get that on the AirTag.

The Pixel Tag measures 28 x 46.1 x 5.4mm, weighs 11.8g with its battery, carries an IP67 rating, and uses a replaceable CR2032 cell rated for more than a year.

Google will sell the Pixel Tag for $29, or four for $99, starting November 11. It works with Pixel Watch and Pixel Buds, so Google’s greater device ecosystem can help you locate your stuff.

At my content capture in Toronto, Canada, I spent time watching how some of these new features came to life.

I think HiLight is a pretty cool feature, but was it absolutely necessary? Probably not. That being said, watching my Google rep show me how it works was pretty cool. The feature itself is a small glowing LED light that is emitted on the camera bar. It turns on when you trigger Gemini, and you can use it for notifications as well.

As the Pro XL was face down on the table, my Google rep spoke out, “Hey Google, can you tell me the weather in Toronto?” Flashing between white and blue as Gemini was thinking, it responded without my Google rep ever having to lift his phone.

With Pixel devices, my attention is usually on the camera, and this year the features are exceptional.

I know my colleague Nick Sutrich will particularly enjoy playing around with Magic Capture. This new feature captures a moving subject and breaks it down into a sequence of sharp, crystal-clear still photos.

I also found the new Translate Video in real time super fascinating. My Google rep showed me a video in Spanish, and as the woman started speaking, the voice I heard was that of a person who dubbed the video into English.

Finally, my absolute favorite feature just got a huge upgrade. Circle to Search in camera mode. You can now take a picture within the Camera and directly use Circle to Search, a very convenient feature.

I’ll also add that the new devices have even more zoom capabilities: the base has 30x zoom, while the Pro models have 120x zoom.

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099, which is $100 more than last year’s Pixel 10 Pro, but you also get more base storage at 256GB, so the pricing still matches last year’s. Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 Pro XL now starts at $1,299 for the same base 256GB storage, so it gets a bit of a price bump, which should be no surprise given the current industry trends.

The Pixel 11 is cute, vibrant, fun, and that’s really what it’s about

I can’t really say much about the base Pixel 11 model because it really didn’t feel like it changed much from previous years. What did catch my eye was the colors.

Google really outdid itself with the fun and vibrant colors. I’m not a huge fan of pink, but the bright magenta pink stood out, and to me, if you were to give your teenage kid or even a young adult one of these phones, then I approve!

While other companies have launched phones this year with mild and muted colors, which I love and appreciate, I think Google had a little fun this year, and I’m glad they did.

Why I never care for the base model is because if I’m going to spend the money on a phone, I want it to have Pro features, and the base model rarely gets them. That said, like the Pro models, the base model is powered by the Tensor G6 with 12GB of RAM, so you’ll still get many of the same features, with some exceptions. That includes the new Gemini Intelligence, which lets the AI handle tasks for you or make suggestions based on your interactions in Messages, At a Glance, and other areas.

However, you’re missing out on other features, like the 120x zoom and HiLight, to name a couple. So, if you're getting this phone for your kid and want them to have a good experience without spending too much or exposing them to too much AI, this is the phone they should be getting.

item.content:encoded:
I think it’s time Google branched out to give people what they need — a Pixel Watch Pro. And I’m saying this because, after playing with the Pixel Watch 5, I’m not sure why the company keeps putting out a new version of the watch every year when not much has really changed.

I want to be very clear: I love the Pixel Watch. I mean, I broke the news that the very first Pixel Watch was found in a restaurant. So you can imagine my excitement when I see new Pixel Watches every year. But now it’s starting to get boring.

Not much has changed, nothing exciting is happening, and the number of Wear OS updates and upgrades doesn’t justify the price increase of the Watch.

Still the same watch

While the form factor of the watch remains the same, Google did come up with some new watch band colors, including olive-toned, magenta-toned, and frost-toned, to match the new Pixel 11 base colors.

Google also didn’t update its chip to the Snapdragon Wear Elite, as Samsung did with its Galaxy Watches. Instead, the new Pixel Watch 5 is still using the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 “Accelerated,” which seems to be a boosted version of the same chip from the Pixel Watch 4.

The look and feel of the new watch is literally the same as the past two generations, and in my opinion nothing really has changed. That’s not fully a bad thing; the Pixel Watch is one of the more gorgeous smartwatches on the market. However, it’s starting to get bland, and something new needs to happen here.

Specs

Wear OS 7

CPU

Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated, Cortex M55 co-processor

Display

Storage

Sensors

Compass, altimeter, red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2) monitoring, multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, multi-path optical heart rate sensor, 3-axis accelerometer, gyroscope, ambient light sensor, electrical sensor to measure skin conductance (cEDA) for body response tracking, far field skin temperature sensor, barometer, and magnetometer.

Battery

45mm: 465mAh, 40 hours with AOD, 72 hours with Battery Saver

Charging

41mm: 15 minutes to 50%, 25 minutes to 80%, 45 minutes to 100%

45mm: 15 minutes to 50%, 30 minutes to 80%, 60 minutes to 100%

Materials

Recycled aluminum

Protection

Custom Corning Gorilla Glass 5, 5ATM, IP68

Band

Dimensions

41mm: 41 x 41 x 12.3mm

45mm: 45 x 45 x 12.3mm

Weight (w/out band)

41mm: 31g

45mm: 36.7g

Colors

Matte Black, Polished Silver, Satine Pyrite, Champagne Gold (41mm)

New features might make the watch worth it

If you were to get the Watch 5, the only reason you should get it is because of the new Gemini and Wear OS features. And many of these features are probably going to take a while to trickle down to the other watches.

The new Insulin Resistance Trends and Blood Pressure Trends features are incredibly compelling. Both have never been on any Pixel Watch before, and both are active features to help monitor your health trends. When I was at my content capture, both features were not available to try out, as they were not ready yet. But I am certain that when the Watch is ready to be shipped, it will be available.

I will also note that my Google rep told me it takes about a month of daily tracking to get trend results, so even if that feature was there at content capture, it would be hard to test without at least 30 days of testing.

Android Central’s Derrek Lee is also very excited about the newly upgraded workout experience, which now includes weight and rep tracking as well as rest timers and a workout builder, making the Watch 5 a more well-rounded fitness companion.

Generative Watch Faces: Your next bff

Honestly, the thing I was most excited about was the new Generative Watch Faces feature. This feature is going to be so fun to play around with, and it uses Google’s Nano Banana to generate.

I tested the feature by asking the watch face to generate pink unicorns, and it actually did. It was super cute and fun, and I think this will be a game-changer for people who like custom watch faces and want to have fun with what their watch looks like.

It’s time for a Pixel Watch Pro

As much as I love the Pixel Watch, it’s time for Google to upgrade what it's doing. I like the new workout features and some of the other features I mentioned above, but I think it’s time Google launched a Pro version of its watches.

It could be something similar to the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 or the Apple Watch Ultra 3, a watch that is much more rugged and geared to serious workout enthusiasts or athletes. In my opinion, the watch could have a deeper focus on fitness and offer something even more compelling for those who would pay the money for it.

As an example, I currently own a Garmin Forerunner 970, and I sought out this watch because I am training for a half marathon. I knew that my training would involve deep stats and workout details that a regular watch might not suffice for. And I think it’s for this very reason Google needs to think about expanding its watch family.

I don’t hate the Pixel, and I think maybe after reading this you might think that, and that is far from how I feel. I love the Pixel; I think it is a robust watch with really great features, but Gen 5 feels boring and flat. I want something more, and I know Google is capable of it.

item.content:encoded:
What you need to know

  • The Pixel Watch 5 looks almost identical to the Pixel Watch 4 and keeps the same W5 Gen 2 chip.
  • Google calls it the W5 Gen 2 Accelerated, but the underlying hardware remains essentially unchanged.
  • You still get 41mm and 45mm models, with Bluetooth, NFC, UWB, and LTE options.
  • New tools for insulin and blood pressure management add meaningful functionality.

Google's smartwatches are slowly gaining momentum, but you wouldn't be able to tell each model apart. That's particularly true this year with the Pixel Watch 5; I read the press release Google shared ahead of launch, and I still don't understand what's new.

The Pixel Watch 5 looks identical to last year's Pixel Watch 4. It has the exact same hardware as well, and Google didn't bother using Qualcomm's Snapdragon Elite Wear platform, which is short-sighted. It instead has the same W5 Gen 2 as last year, but it's now called the Gen 2 Accelerated, so make of that what you will.

Like previous years, you get two sizes: 41mm and 45mm. There's Bluetooth, NFC, UWB, and Satellite SOS in select countries, and Google will continue to sell cellular-enabled LTE models. You get similar colors as last year, and the chassis is made out of recycled materials, just like Google's phones. There are new bands though, and they're in vibrant colors.

You still get 5ATM and IP68 water resistance, and it should hold up to everyday wear and tear just as well as its predecessors.

That doesn't mean there isn't anything new. Google is debuting features to manage insulin and blood pressure resistance, and they're bound to be useful. There's a slate of new Gemini features as well, along with everything new in Wear OS. Here's the full list of the watch's health and fitness features:

  • Health Guardian suite (Irregular Rhythm Notifications / AFib, high/low heart rate alerts)
  • Monthly blood pressure trends & insulin resistance trends
  • Multi-path optical heart rate sensor & SpO2 monitoring
  • ECG app & Skin conductance (cEDA) tracking
  • Far-field skin temperature sensor
  • Google Health Coach integration (powered by Gemini)
  • 50+ tracked exercises with custom HIIT/strength routine syncing
  • Readiness Score & Key Metrics post-workout view
  • Sleep Breathing Quality (minute-by-minute SpO2 analysis)
  • Stage tracking (Awake, REM, Light, Deep) & Sleep Score
  • Bedtime Automations, Smart Wake Alarms, Morning Brief
  • Breathing Emergency Detection (EU only)
  • Loss of Pulse alerts
  • Satellite SOS communication
  • Safety Check, Emergency Sharing, Fall Detection, Car Crash Detection

Oh, and I like the feature that lets you generate watch faces using AI, and it is pretty cool. But that alone doesn't justify buying a new watch, and the Pixel Watch 4 should get the feature anyway at some point in the future.

If the Pixel Watch 5 doesn't look particularly noteworthy, it's because the hardware itself hasn't changed to any measurable degree. This is like the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2025 all over again, and Google needs to do better to differentiate its smartwatch -- as AC EiC Shruti Shekar said in her hands-on post, it's time we got a Pixel Watch Pro.

item.content:encoded:
What you need to know

  • The Pixel 11 Pro Fold goes official, and it is nearly 10% lighter and about 1mm thinner than its predecessor.
  • A glass-fiber composite back, ceramic outer cover glass, and new gearless hinge make the Fold three times more durable than the previous model.
  • HiLight is one of the headline features, designed to use different colors for calls from favorite contacts and provide visual cues when Gemini is being used hands-free.
  • The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is up for preorder and arrives on August 20.

If you were hoping Google would chase Samsung down the rabbit hole of razor-thin foldables, you're about to be disappointed. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is here, and while it’s much lighter and thinner than its predecessor, it’s not trying to win a slimming contest with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which weighs 201g.

Google says the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is nearly 10% lighter and about 1mm thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, along with a new hinge and stronger materials. That said, it does weigh 239g, so Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is still a lot more portable. Samsung’s new Fold is also 9.7mm thick when closed versus the Pixel’s 10.1mm.

Google’s answer is durability. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a glass-fiber composite back, a ceramic cover glass on the outer display, and a new gearless hinge. The company says the combo makes it three-times more durable than its predecessor, while the bigger bend radius and thicker inner glass of the hinge are meant to improve the crease. The phone still has an IP68 rating, too.

The screens have been upgraded. You get a 6.5-inch 1080 x 2342 outer OLED and an 8-inch 2076 x 2152 inner OLED that both run from 1Hz to 120Hz and peak at 3,600 nits.

Powerful hardware

Inside, Google stuffs the Fold with 16GB of RAM, Tensor G6, and up to 1TB of Zoned UFS storage, a new flash storage technology for mobile devices that segregates data into separate logical “zones” to enhance long-term performance and boost storage longevity.

The battery capacity is 4,750mAh and is rated for over 24 hours, and 30W wired charging will supposedly get you to 50% in around 30 minutes. Pixelsnap also supports up to 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.

Photography gets a substantial push, too. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a 48MP main camera, a 10.5MP ultrawide with autofocus and macro focus, and a 10.8MP 5x telephoto, with up to 30x Super Zoom. That gives Google a clear zoom-focused angle against Samsung’s dual 50MP rear cameras on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers up to 10x digital zoom.

Google is also making the new Fold feel more like a real productivity tool. App bubbles are designed for the big screen, and Split Screen, Drag and Drop, Instant View, and improved Made You Look animations are still here. The new sign-to-text translation leverages the camera, Gboard, and Live Transcribe to convert American Sign Language into text on the outer display.

Then there's HiLight, a new LED system built around the camera flash. It can flicker in a variety of colors for calls from your favorite contacts and provide visual cues during hands-free Gemini interactions, with more notification features coming soon.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is available to preorder now in Olive and Obsidian colorways. It starts at $1,899 and will be released on August 20.
